---
title: "Fixing code you didn't write"
---

![What the program you're handed already draws: close to the real symbol, but the interlocking isn't quite right yet.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstropek/ts-web-playground/main/exercises/0010-Basics/olympic_rings_advanced.png){width=360}

This time you won't write the program from scratch. You'll be handed one that someone else already wrote, where the five Olympic rings don't quite link up, and your job is to spot why and repair it, until each ring weaves over one neighbour and under the other the way it does on the real symbol.

So far, every program in this course started with you (or your AI) writing
the code. This exercise turns the situation around: you get a program that
someone else wrote. It almost works, but not quite, and your job is to find
the problem and fix it.

Don't underestimate this exercise. Professional programmers spend most of
their time exactly like this: reading code they didn't write, understanding
it, and carefully changing it. Whoever wrote the original, a colleague, an
AI, or you-three-weeks-ago, the skill is the same.

{{< tutor tutor-introduction >}}

## The puzzle: weaving the rings {#sec-weaving}

In the Olympic Rings exercise you drew five overlapping rings and ignored
*how* they overlap. Now look closely at the real symbol: the rings are
woven together. Follow the blue ring with your eyes: where it crosses the
yellow ring, it passes **over** it in one crossing and **under** it in the
other.

Here's the catch: you can't draw that with five full circles. The computer
paints shapes in order, so a later circle always lies completely on top of
an earlier one. A full circle can be over or under a neighbor, but never
both at once.

The trick is to stop thinking of a ring as one shape. Split it into
**arcs**: draw most of the ring early, and paint the small missing piece
*after* the neighbor ring, right where it has to pass over. The eye sees a
woven ring; the code sees a few arcs in a well-chosen order. The layering
rule you know, later statements paint over earlier ones, is exactly what
makes this work.

## Read before you change {#sec-read}

The starter code of the exercise already solves most of this puzzle. Before
you change anything, spend time understanding it:

1. **Run the program** and put its output next to the target image. Compare
   crossing by crossing: where do the rings weave correctly, and where not?
   Finding the difference between "what it should do" and "what it does" is
   always the first step of fixing a program.
2. **Read the code from top to bottom.** You know every command in it,
   including `arc` and `angleMode(DEGREES)` from the smiley exercise. The
   comments tell you which statement belongs to which ring.
3. **Study how the finished rings do it.** The blue and black rings are
   already woven correctly, and they show the pattern: a ring appears
   several times in the code, as arcs, with other rings drawn in between.
   Work out which piece of the ring each arc paints. The angle diagram from
   the arcs chapter helps: 0° points right, and angles grow clockwise.

Reading code this way takes patience, and that's normal. Understanding a
program you didn't write is slower than writing your own, even for
professionals.

## Fix the red ring {#sec-fix}

The broken part is the red ring: it's still drawn as one full `circle`, so
it can't weave with its neighbor. That's your repair job:

1. Look at the target image and decide where the red ring must pass over
   and where it must pass under the ring it crosses.
2. Replace the red `circle` with arcs, following the same pattern that the
   blue and black rings use. Think about the angles each arc needs, and
   about *where in the code* each arc has to stand: before or after the
   neighbor it crosses.
3. Change a little, run, compare with the image, and repeat. If a change
   makes things worse, `Ctrl` + `Z` takes you back.

Be careful to change only what's broken. The other four rings are correct,
and a fix that breaks something else is not a fix. Comparing the picture
with the target after every run is your safety net.

When the five rings finally weave like the original, take a moment: you've
just read a foreign program, understood a genuinely tricky idea in it, and
repaired it without breaking the rest. That's real programming work.
